steps.explanationAfterStep: An irreversible deprotonation: hydrogen gas escapes. 18-crown-6 wraps round the potassium ion and pulls it away from the oxygen, leaving a 'naked', highly reactive alkoxide.

steps.caption: Hydrogen gas bubbles out of the solution.

steps.explanationAfterStep: A Cope rearrangement of the alkoxide. The O⁻ pushes electron density into the breaking C–C bond and weakens it, so the reaction runs at room temperature instead of 200 °C or more: Evans measured rate increases of 10¹⁰ to 10¹⁷. The product is an enolate, so the reaction is irreversible. The transition state is chair-like, as in every Cope rearrangement. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the drawings carry no wedges and no E/Z marks.

steps.caption: Aqueous ammonium chloride is added at the end.

steps.explanationAfterStep: Protonation on carbon gives the ketone. The neutral oxy-Cope (heating the alcohol itself) gives the enol, which tautomerises to the same ketone.

title: Anionic oxy-Cope rearrangement
subtitle: A potassium alkoxide speeds a [3,3] shift by up to 10¹⁷ times and gives an enolate
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 35
D. A. Evans and A. M. Golob, J. Am. Chem. Soc., 1975, 97, 4765

alcohol.caption: 3-methylhexa-1,5-dien-3-ol and potassium hydride (18-crown-6 in THF, not drawn)
hintTiers: KH is a base: H⁻ is a strong base and a very poor nucleophile. What is the most acidic hydrogen here?
Hydride takes the O–H proton: hydrogen gas and a potassium alkoxide. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: from the hydride lone pair to the hydrogen on oxygen. Arrow 2: from the O–H bond onto oxygen.
alcohol.learnerPrompt: Potassium hydride is added to the alcohol. Draw the first step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Potassium hydride does not deliver hydride to carbon: it is a base. It removes the O–H proton, and hydrogen gas bubbles away.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: hydride takes the proton. Now let the O–H pair stay on oxygen. One more arrow.

alkoxide.caption: the potassium alkoxide and hydrogen gas

curled-alkoxide.caption: the alkoxide, drawn curled so its two alkene ends meet
hintTiers: Number the 1,5-diene from one alkene end: 1=2–3–4–5=6, with the oxygen on carbon 3. Six atoms, six electrons, one step.

The σ bond between the oxygen-bearing carbon and its CH₂ neighbour breaks, the two alkene CH₂ ends bond together, and both π bonds move one place inwards. Three arrows. The O⁻ itself does not need an arrow.

Arrow 1: from the vinyl C=C π bond (next to the oxygen-bearing carbon) to a new bond between the two terminal CH₂ groups. Arrow 2: from the bond between the oxygen-bearing carbon and its CH₂ neighbour to the bond between the oxygen-bearing carbon and the vinyl CH. Arrow 3: from the other C=C π bond to the bond between its CH and the CH₂ that lost the σ bond.
curled-alkoxide.learnerPrompt: At room temperature the alkoxide rearranges within minutes. Draw the single step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking that C–C bond onto carbon would give an allyl anion and a ketone. In the oxy-Cope the bond breaks only as the new C–C bond forms, in one cyclic step, and the pair goes into the new C=C.
That bond is next to a C=C. In a [3,3] shift the bond that breaks is the central one of the 1,5-diene: between the oxygen-bearing carbon and its CH₂ neighbour.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Two of three. The CH₂ at the other end has bonded but still has its π bond: that π pair moves inwards to the CH₂ that lost the σ bond.

enolate-and-ammonium-chloride.caption: the enolate with aqueous ammonium chloride
hintTiers: An enolate can be protonated on oxygen or on carbon. Which gives the stable product directly?
The C=C π bond takes the proton on carbon, and the oxygen lone pair re-forms the C=O. Three arrows.
Arrow 1: from the enolate C=C π bond to a hydrogen of the ammonium ion. Arrow 2: from that N–H bond onto nitrogen. Arrow 3: from a lone pair on oxygen to its bond with carbon (it becomes C=O).
enolate-and-ammonium-chloride.learnerPrompt: Ammonium chloride is a weak acid. Protonate the enolate to give the ketone.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: That gives the enol, a real intermediate if the proton goes to oxygen first, but it soon tautomerises. Here protonate on carbon to reach the ketone in one step.

conditionsLabel: KH, 18-crown-6, THF, room temperature · then aqueous NH₄Cl
mechanismSummary: The oxy-Cope rearrangement is a Cope rearrangement of a 1,5-diene carrying OH on carbon 3. Converted to its potassium alkoxide (KH, with 18-crown-6 to hold the potassium ion away), it rearranges up to 10¹⁷ times faster, at or below room temperature: the anionic oxy-Cope. The [3,3] shift goes through a chair-like transition state and gives an enolate, so it is irreversible; work-up gives a δ,ε-unsaturated ketone. With 1,2-divinylcycloalkanols it expands a ring by four carbons. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the drawings carry no wedges and no E/Z marks.
